terms.gloss: be on good terms with someone, be in favour with
terms.grammar: grātia, grātiae f., with cum and the ablative
evidence: Cic. Verr. 1.51: ut is cum populō Rōmānō et in laude et in grātiā esse possit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin is “in favour with” someone: in grātiā sum cum frātre. To make it up again is in grātiam redīre (see favour).

terms.gloss: a close bond, close friendship or kinship
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.5.176: nūlla tibi cum istō cognātiō, nūlla necessitūdō (Lewis & Short s.v. cognātiō)
Traupman 109: mihi cum (+ abl.) magna necessitūdō est

terms.comment: Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase.

sources: Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 109.: p. 320.
